retired.question: Under which catalogue number is the tomb of Tutankhamun listed in the Valley of the Kings?
retired.why: The tomb's catalogue number KV62 is a dry reference code, the least engaging question of the Tutankhamun article.

retired.question: From which African state did Eritrea break away as a separate country in 1993 after an independence referendum?
retired.why: Eritrea's 1993 secession from Ethiopia is already asked in the article on late-20th-century secessions, so this question was a near-duplicate.

retired.question: Who were the “Big Three” at the start of the Potsdam Conference in July 1945?
retired.why: The Potsdam 'Big Three' question nearly repeats the Yalta one, differing only by Truman for Roosevelt.

retired.question: In which year did Margaret Thatcher and Zhao Ziyang sign the Joint Declaration that fixed Hong Kong's return to China?
retired.why: A bare year lookup (1984) for the Joint Declaration, the dullest question of the Hong Kong and Macau article.

retired.question: What was the surname of the German couple who discovered the glacier mummy Ötzi near the Tisenjoch pass in September 1991?
retired.why: The surname of the hikers who found Ötzi is an incidental detail rather than real trivia about the Iceman.

retired.question: Who, as leader of the Islamic Revolution, overthrew the Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, in 1979?
retired.why: Khomeini led a popular revolution, not a coup, so the question did not fit an article about Cold War coups.

retired.question: Emperor Joseph II, Marie Antoinette's eldest brother, was the son of which emperor from the House of Lorraine?
retired.why: Asking for Joseph II's father, Francis I Stephen, was the most forced link in the article's family-tree chain.

retired.question: Which country was the first Soviet republic to declare its independence from the Soviet Union, on 11 March 1990?
retired.why: Lithuania's declaration of 11 March 1990 falls outside the year 1989 that the article is about.

retired.question: To which territory did the United States give up its claim in the Adams–Onís Treaty of 1819, in which it gained Florida?
retired.why: The Adams–Onís question asked for a territory the US gave up rather than acquired, a confusing and forced fit for an article on buying land.

retired.question: Which Aztec ruler received the Spaniards in Tenochtitlan in 1519?
retired.why: Moctezuma II receiving the Spaniards repeats a ruler already asked about in the article on rulers at the edge of conquest.

retired.question: Which war raged from 28 July 1914 to 11 November 1918 and claimed around 17 million lives?
retired.why: Identifying the First World War from its dates is the most obvious and least rewarding of the article's date lookups.

retired.question: In which country was women's suffrage at federal level introduced only in 1971 by a referendum?
retired.why: It asked for Switzerland's 1971 federal women's suffrage, which the printed card of the same article already asks.

retired.question: Who claimed at a press conference on 15 June 1961: „Nobody has any intention of building a wall“?
retired.why: Its answer, Walter Ulbricht, is given away by the printed question of the same article quoting his 'nobody intends to build a wall' remark.

retired.question: Which Israeli ambassador in Washington delivered David Ben-Gurion's offer of the presidency to Albert Einstein in 1952?
retired.why: The ambassador who carried the presidency offer, Abba Eban, is a forced side detail of the Einstein story.

retired.question: Which word stood for the letter K in the spelling table of 1950, which DIN 5009 cited until its 2022 revision?
retired.why: Kaufmann for K is an uneventful entry of the 1950 table with no political story behind it, the weakest of the spelling-alphabet questions.

retired.question: How many hours a day at most could young people under 16 work in Prussian factories under the Regulativ of 1839?
retired.why: The ten-hour limit for young workers repeats the 1839 child-labour regulation that the printed card already asks about, as a dull number.

retired.question: What was the Allied crossing point on Friedrichstraße between East and West Berlin called, named after the letter C in the NATO alphabet?
retired.why: Checkpoint Charlie is already asked by a printed card in the article on the building of the Wall, so this was a duplicate.

retired.question: In which square in Beijing were the pro-democracy protests bloodily crushed in 1989?
retired.why: Tiananmen Square is already asked by a printed card in the article on 1989, so this question was a duplicate.

retired.question: Which city in northern Syria was regarded as the „capital“ of the Islamic State from 2014 until its recapture in 2017?
retired.why: Raqqa as the Islamic State's capital is already asked in the article on the cities of the caliphate.

retired.question: Between which two countries was the Falklands War over an island group in the South Atlantic fought in 1982?
retired.why: The Falklands War pairing is already asked by a printed card in the companion article on wars between two countries.

retired.question: Which event triggered the Second World War in 1939?
retired.why: The German invasion of Poland as the start of the Second World War is already asked in the article on invasions of a neighbour.

retired.question: In which city did the Monday demonstrations begin in autumn 1989 that accelerated the collapse of the GDR?
retired.why: Leipzig's Monday demonstrations of 1989 duplicate a question in the 1989 article and stand outside this article's West German 1980s protests.

retired.question: Which country fought Egypt, Jordan and Syria in the Six-Day War of June 1967?
retired.why: Israel in the Six-Day War is an obvious answer already covered by the article on the century's wars, so it was the weakest question here.

retired.question: Who led independent India from 1947 as its first prime minister?
retired.why: Nehru becoming prime minister has nothing to do with a march, so the question did not fit the article.
